lessons.title: What is a deepfake, and what is not?
lessons.subtitle: Not every generated image is one

sections.title: Three invented cases
sections.content:
1. A manipulated video puts words in a known person's mouth she never said.
2. A fraud call uses a cloned voice to demand a transfer under time pressure.
3. An account builds trust with a fully generated profile picture and an invented biography.

Cases one and two can be deepfakes in law, because they deceptively reproduce an existing person or event. The invented face in case three is synthetic content, but not automatically a deepfake under the AI Regulation, as long as it resembles no existing person or entity.

In none of the cases do appearance or sound prove authenticity or manipulation.

sections.title: What the law calls a deepfake
sections.content:
Article 3(60) of the AI Regulation defines a deepfake more narrowly than everyday use: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing people, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

The definition describes the result and its deceptive effect. Conventional editing can deceive too, but falls under it only when the content is AI-generated or AI-manipulated.

Techniques include face swapping, lip synchronisation, speech synthesis, voice cloning and generative image and video models. The reference material needed depends on the technique; no fixed number of images or minutes of audio exists.

sections.title: Article 50: marking and disclosure
sections.content:
Article 50 of the AI Regulation asks different things of two roles:

- Providers of covered generative systems must, as a general rule, mark synthetic output in machine-readable form as artificially generated or manipulated.
- Deployers who generate or manipulate a deepfake and disclose it must, as a general rule, state visibly that the content was artificially generated or manipulated. Evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works get an adapted disclosure; further statutory exceptions have to be assessed.

Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. For systems already on the market before that date, paragraph 2 applies from 2 December 2026 under the transition in Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. A marking can support provenance; its absence proves no authenticity, because markings can be removed and exceptions can apply.

Sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(60) and Article 50; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Article 1(39)(b).

quiz.questionText: Which statement matches the AI Regulation's deepfake definition?

answerOptions.text: Every fully generated image is a deepfake, whatever its subject
Only content about public figures can be a deepfake
The term always requires particular software and a fixed amount of training data
The content is AI-generated or manipulated, resembles something existing, and would falsely appear authentic or truthful

quiz.explanation: Article 3(60) needs all three marks: AI generation or manipulation, resemblance to something existing, and a false impression of authenticity or truth.

quiz.questionText: Which technical statement about deepfakes is correct?

answerOptions.text: Deepfakes arise only through manual face swapping
Face swapping, lip synchronisation, speech synthesis and generative models can be involved
Every deepfake requires thousands of reference images
Only state actors can run the necessary techniques

quiz.explanation: The reference data and handwork needed depend on the technique. No universal minimum exists.

quiz.questionText: Since when has Article 50 of the AI Regulation generally applied?

answerOptions.text: From 2 February 2025
From 2 August 2026
From 1 January 2027
The marking duty has applied since 2020 under the GDPR

quiz.explanation: Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. For generative systems already on the market before then, the transition for marking under paragraph 2 runs to 2 December 2026.

lessons.title: How to check provenance and context
lessons.subtitle: Source work, not a detector verdict

sections.title: Tools for tracing provenance
sections.content:
No tool tells you whether an image is true. Three tool classes give clues to its origin:

1. Reverse image search: Google Lens and TinEye (tineye.com) can show earlier or similar appearances. An early hit points to context, not automatically to the original source.
2. Video decomposition: InVID/WeVerify (weverify.eu) can split videos into keyframes, trigger reverse searches and show available metadata. Whether a video is true, the extension does not decide.
3. Provenance data: Content Credentials or other signed provenance information can document editing steps and issuers. Missing provenance does not prove manipulation; where it exists, check validity and issuer.

Upload confidential, intimate or personal content only after checking data protection, terms of use and local alternatives.

sections.title: Before you believe a post
sections.content:
1. Pin the claim: what should the content prove, when and where was it supposedly made?
2. Open the source: the earliest reachable post, the complete video, the account or outlet behind it. A screenshot without a link is no reliable source.
3. Cross-check context: compare date, place, language, weather, visible signs and the uncut sequence with independent sources.
4. Look for provenance: use reverse search or keyframes to compare concrete image details instead of similar motifs.
5. Bound the result: record what is confirmed, disproved or open. "Not verified" is a permissible result.

Oddities in hands, hair, blinking, light or compression justify a second look. They do not work as a checklist, because generators change and camera, cut or compression leave the same traces.

sections.title: What a detector's percentage means
sections.content:
A detector's percentage is a model-dependent estimate and not automatically a calibrated probability for your case. Its worth depends on training data, tested generators, compression, crop, post-processing and threshold.

- A negative result establishes no authenticity. The content can sit outside the known test distribution, or be altered.
- A positive result establishes no manipulation. Genuine recordings can trigger features the model misreads.

Use detectors as an extra signal at most. To publish, accuse or litigate, you need traceable provenance, context, further evidence and, where necessary, specialist forensic analysis.

quiz.questionText: What can a reverse image search actually contribute?

answerOptions.text: Proof that an image was generated with AI
Automatic confirmation of all EXIF metadata
Earlier or similar appearances, and with them clues about context
Reliable identification of every person shown

quiz.explanation: The search finds indexed identical or similar images and so shows earlier uses or other contexts. The earliest hit is not necessarily the original source.

quiz.questionText: What beats a list of visual artefacts?

answerOptions.text: Counting fingers in a single frame
Treating poor image quality as proof of manipulation
Treating a missing watermark as proof of authenticity
Checking source, full context, earlier appearances and independent confirmation

quiz.explanation: Visual oddities change with every generator generation and show up in genuine, compressed or edited footage too. Source and context give evidence others can check.

quiz.questionText: What does a negative detector result mean?

answerOptions.text: The image is certainly genuine
A real person took the image
This detector found no sufficient signal under its conditions; authenticity is not established
The tool could not process the image

quiz.explanation: The result holds only for this model, this threshold and the content tested. Unknown techniques or post-processing can change it.

lessons.title: What to do when you find a deepfake
lessons.subtitle: Preserve and report without sharing

sections.title: What to do after you find it
sections.content:
1. Do not spread it: no public sharing, quoting or comment, even with a warning. Where safe, save URL, account name, timestamp and a screenshot locally.
2. Check first, accuse later: a suspicion is no finding. Use the source check from Lesson 2.
3. Report precisely: through the platform's current reporting route, with the URL and the possible legal or policy breach. Article 16 of the Digital Services Act obliges hosting services to offer an easily accessible electronic notice mechanism for allegedly illegal content. Sufficiently precise notices have to be handled and decided in a timely, diligent, objective and non-arbitrary way; no duty to remove every reported item follows from that.
4. Tell the affected person privately: send source location and evidence without passing on the content.
5. On a possible crime or immediate danger, involve the police: the competent online police station is at polizei.de; in an acute emergency, call the emergency number.

sections.title: Where your complaint goes
sections.content:
Where you turn depends on who breached what. A platform notice under the DSA, a criminal complaint and an AI Act complaint have different recipients and conditions. For Article 50, check marking by providers and disclosure by deployers separately, each with the exceptions and transition rules from Lesson 1.

Article 85 lets you complain to the competent market surveillance authority. Under the KI-MIG that is generally the Bundesnetzagentur, as market surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints body, unless a sector authority is competent. Use the officially published authority channel that is current.

Sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 50 and 85; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; KI-MIG.

sections.title: When your image or voice is hit
sections.content:
Under Section 22 KUG, portraits may be distributed or publicly displayed only with the consent of the person shown. The exceptions in Section 23 KUG and the balancing under Section 23(2) still need checking. Whether a deepfake infringes these rights, and what claim follows, depends on content, context and distribution route.

Section 22 KUG does not protect your voice alone. With cloned or manipulated audio, the general right of personality, data protection law and civil or criminal provisions can apply, depending on use. Nobody can promise a particular legal consequence without examining your case.

Preserve source location and evidence without passing the content on. verbraucherzentrale.de and klicksafe.de give a first orientation; qualified media-law advice assesses your claims.

quiz.questionText: What do you do first when you hit a suspected deepfake?

answerOptions.text: Forward the video straight to every media outlet you know for analysis
Do not share publicly; preserve the source location and available evidence locally
Call the Federal Criminal Police Office immediately
Post your own fact-check on social media

quiz.explanation: Every public pass-along grows the reach, including the well-meant kind. Preserve evidence first, then report.

quiz.questionText: How do you find the complaint route for a possible Article 50 breach?

answerOptions.text: Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA)
Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin)
Always write straight to the Bundesnetzagentur, whatever the sector and published competence
Check official Bundesnetzagentur information, possible sector competence and the currently published authority channel

quiz.explanation: Under the KI-MIG the Bundesnetzagentur is competent unless a sector authority is. So first check the current official competence information and the published authority channel.

answerOptions.text: The right to publish your own works of art
The photographer's copyright in their pictures
Portraits may be distributed or publicly shown only with consent; Section 23 sets the exceptions
The right to delete AI-generated images

quiz.explanation: Section 22 KUG holds the consent rule, Section 23 KUG the exceptions and balancing of interests. Whether a deepfake infringes a right is decided case by case.
